Note::base64_encode¶

Back to Note API Reference

Signature¶

Note Note::base64_encode() const

Encode Every Cell As Standard Base64¶

base64_encode() replaces each text cell with its Base64 transfer encoding, using the standard alphabet (A-Z, a-z, 0-9, +, /) and = padding (RFC 4648 §4). It is the method to reach for when a Note has to travel through a channel that only carries printable ASCII — a JSON string, a URL fragment budget permitting, an HTTP header, a log line, a config value.

The input is treated as a byte sequence, not as characters: a cell holding "café" is encoded from its four UTF-8 bytes (63 61 66 C3 A9 — five bytes), so the result depends on the exact bytes, not on how many characters they render as. This is why the encoded length grows in blocks of four output characters per three input bytes, with = padding when the final block is short.

The operation is shape-preserving and cell-independent: the result has the same rank and extents as the input, each cell encoded on its own, and a new allocation is returned. The result is a UTF-8-mode Note (the Base64 alphabet is ASCII). An empty cell encodes to an empty cell.

base64_decode is the exact inverse for any Note produced here.

Example 1: A Scalar¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(pluss::make_note("Hello, Note").base64_encode())
          << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[], dim=0, numel=1, encoding=utf8)
"SGVsbG8sIE5vdGU="

Example 2: Padding Follows The Input Length¶

const pluss::Note n =
    pluss::make_note({"abc", "ab", "a", ""}).base64_encode();
std::cout << n << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[4], dim=1, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
["YWJj", "YWI=", "YQ==", ""]

Three input bytes give a full four-character block with no padding; two bytes give one =; one byte gives two =. An empty cell stays empty.

Example 3: Multi-Byte UTF-8 Is Encoded From Its Bytes¶

pluss::note::print(std::cout,
                   pluss::make_note({"café", "€"}).base64_encode())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["Y2Fmw6k=", "4oKs"]

"café" is five bytes (é is two), and "€" is three bytes, so they encode to eight and four Base64 characters respectively.

Example 4: Shape Is Preserved¶

std::cout << pluss::note::print(
    pluss::make_note({{"one", "two"}, {"three", "four"}}).base64_encode())
    << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2, 2], dim=2, numel=4, encoding=utf8)
[
  ["b25l", "dHdv"], 
  ["dGhyZWU=", "Zm91cg=="]
]

Example 5: Round-Trips Through base64_decode¶

const pluss::Note original = pluss::make_note({"payload", "café"});
std::cout << original.base64_encode().base64_decode() << "\n";

Output¶

Note(shape=[2], dim=1, numel=2, encoding=utf8)
["payload", "café"]

base64_decode() recovers the exact original bytes.

See Also¶

  • pluss::coden::Note::base64_decode: the inverse.

  • Note::url_encode: percent-encoding for the same “make it ASCII-safe” goal, keyed to URL syntax instead of transfer size.

  • Note::TexAccessor::escape: escaping for a specific consumer (TeX) rather than a general binary-safe encoding.
